title: Mastering the Fourth: Superior Oblique Palsy
summary: The definitive clinical guide to Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) Palsy, covering the complex anatomy, the legendary 3-step test, and advanced surgical management of vertical diplopia.

sections.title: Definition & Anatomical Peculiarities
content: The Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) is the thinnest cranial nerve (~2,400 axons).
Longest intracranial course (approx. 75mm) making it highly susceptible to trauma.
The only cranial nerve to exit the brainstem dorsally.
The only cranial nerve where all lower motor neuron fibers decussate (in the superior medullary velum).
Innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle, which depresses, abducts, and incyclotorts the eye.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Vertical Diplopia: Worse on down-gaze (reading) and looking away from the side of the lesion.
Torsional Diplopia: Images appear tilted.
Compensatory Head Tilt: To the opposite shoulder to minimize diplopia (Bielschowsky's sign).
Aesthenopia: Vague eye strain during near work.
Facial Asymmetry: Often seen in long-standing congenital cases (hypoplasia of the affected side).

sections.title: Parks-Bielschowsky Three-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is Hypertropic in primary position (e.g., Right Hypertropia).
Step 2: Determine if the Hypertropia increases in Right or Left Gaze (e.g., increases in Left Gaze).
Step 3: Determine if the Hypertropia increases on Right or Left Head Tilt (e.g., increases on Right Tilt).
Conclusion: If RHT is worse in Left Gaze and Right Tilt = Right SO Palsy.

rows: Shows head tilt (FAT Scan - Family Album Tomography)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Orthoptic measurements (Prism Cover Test) in 9 positions of gaze.
2. Double Maddox Rod test: Quantify excyclotorsion (usually >5-10° in bilateral).
3. Hess Chart / Lancaster Red-Green: Documentation of paretic field.
4. Neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbit): If non-vasculopathic, non-traumatic, or associated with other CN signs.
5. Systemic screen: BP, HbA1c, Myasthenia screen (Ice test/Tensilon) if mimicry suspected.

rows: Associated with brainstem signs, tilt is non-comitant

sections.title: Bilateral IV Nerve Palsy Red Flags
content: Excyclotorsion > 10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
Reversing Hypertropia (RHT in left gaze, LHT in right gaze).
Significant V-pattern Esotropia (>15PD difference).
Positive Bielschowsky tilt test to both sides.
Chin-down head position.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Inferior Oblique (IO) Weakening: Recession, Myectomy, or Anteriorization. Used for Class I/III.
Superior Oblique (SO) Tuck: Tightening the tendon. Used for lax tendons or Class II.
Harada-Ito Procedure: Splitting the SO tendon and moving the anterior portion anteriorly/laterally to correct excyclotorsion.
Ipsilateral Superior Rectus (SR) Recession: For small deviations in primary gaze.
Contralateral Inferior Rectus (IR) Recession: For deviations larger in down-gaze.

content.explanation: IV Nerve, 4000 (actually 2.4k) fibers, 4th decade (ischemic), 4 types of surgery. Remember SO: Superior Oblique = SIN (Superior muscles are Incyclotortors).

sections.title: Key High-Yield Pearls
content: The 'Masked Bilateral' phenomenon: Operating on one eye reveals a palsy in the other that was previously hidden by suppression.
Superior Medullary Velum is the most common site of traumatic injury due to decussating fibers.
Non-traumatic, non-vasculopathic isolated IV palsy in adults should prompt neuroimaging to rule out schwannoma or meningioma.
Prism therapy (Base-down over the hypertropic eye) is excellent for stable, small-angle acquired palsies.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Most ischemic IV nerve palsies resolve spontaneously within 3 to 6 months. Surgical success rates are high, but patients must be warned about the possibility of 'iatrogenic Brown syndrome' following an over-zealous SO tuck. Recurrence is rare unless the underlying cause (e.g., tumor) progresses.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: CISS/FIESTA MRI sequences: High-resolution imaging now allows direct visualization of the trochlear nerve to detect atrophy or aplasia.
Botulinum Toxin: Used in the acute phase into the antagonist IO muscle to prevent contracture and alleviate symptoms while waiting for recovery.
Computerized Strabismus Mapping: Improved pre-operative planning for complex multi-muscle surgery.
